To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) energy savings can be obtained from offloading method execution to the server; (2) the compilation energy is a dominant factor in determining the overall energy consumption of a mobile client; (3) the energy consumption for executing a method is a function of both the computation and the communication energies; and (4) the energy consumption of a method is not necessarily correlated with its execution time.

(1) offloading method compilation to the server reduces the energy consumed by the mobile client; (2) offloading method execution to the server reduces energy consumed by the device; (3) the optimal method compilation strategy depends on the method execution strategy and vice-versa; (4) the optimal method execution strategy depends on the compilation strategy; and (5) the optimal method invocation strategy depends on the application and the method characteristics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of a framework that allows the server to take over some of the execution and compilation tasks of the mobile client in order to save energy.
the development of energy-aware compilation and execution strategies for Java-enabled mobile devices in a wireless network.

the following: (i) how to dynamically decide where and how to execute a Java method in a mobile client; (ii) how to offload the compilation of a Java method to a server; and (iii) how to dynamically adjust the level of optimization for a Java method based on its energy consumption.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

our proposed framework can significantly save energy for a wide range of Java-enabled mobile devices, especially when the server has a higher computational power and the mobile client is battery-powered.
the proposed framework can save energy by offloading some computations to the server, but it is not always beneficial.
this thesis work has successfully addressed the problem of energy-efficient compilation and execution of Java applications in mobile environments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

it provides a novel energy-aware framework that allows the server to offload some computations (method execution and dynamic compilation), which normally consume energy on mobile devices, and to execute these computations remotely.
our framework provides a mechanism to offload method execution and dynamic code compilation to the resource-rich remote host to save energy in wireless devices.
it provides a framework to dynamically decide the best place to compile and execute Java applications on mobile devices.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the proposed energy-aware framework can reduce the overall energy consumption of a Java application by 20-50% compared to the baseline (i.e., the default execution model of the Java virtual machine).

it is possible to significantly reduce the energy consumed by the mobile device by offloading the method execution and dynamic just-in-time compilation to the server, without compromising the user experience.

it is possible to significantly reduce the energy consumption of a mobile client while executing a Java application by offloading method executions to the server and by dynamically choosing the most suitable execution model for each method.
